evidence.fact: Commercial AI record-retrieval platforms for law firms say they automate authorization validation, sending requests to US providers, follow-up, and sorting the records that come back. They also connect to case-management tools like Clio. These are vendor claims and say human oversight is still needed.

Releasing medical records needs a HIPAA authorization signed by the patient or a qualified personal representative, or else a subpoena or court order. A human has to supply this step, and an attorney cannot sign it just because they are on the case.

Retrieval guides for lawyers say the process starts only once a HIPAA-compliant authorization, subpoena, or court order is in place. After that, requests go to each provider's records department and have to be followed up until the records arrive.

Commercial retail space-planning software (LEAFIO) builds planograms automatically from sales data, ABC analysis, turnover and user-defined rules, and auto-calculates facings. These are vendor claims.
DotActiv markets AI planogram generation with batch creation of size variants that follow layout rules, plus an LLM category-management assistant. These are vendor claims.

Retail layouts are bound by occupancy, egress width and travel-distance code rules, such as the 75-ft sprinklered mercantile limit cited from IBC Table 1006.2.1 in a practitioner forum. A human with knowledge of the actual site still has to check compliance and fit before the layout is built in the store.

Commercial EHS platforms such as Notify Spark (launched October 2025), Benchmark Gensuite and EHS4Safety already use AI to handle accident reports, root-cause analysis and workers' compensation workflows. That covers the documentation, analysis and reporting steps.

Employers must collect information from injured employees, witnesses and treating health professionals and finish OSHA Form 301 within 7 days. An employer's designated representative can complete the form, so the law does not appear to require a specific licensed signer. The accident-scene inspection and in-person witness interviews still need a human on site.

A state workers' compensation report can count as an equivalent form if it captures the required information. That lets an agent draft one report that covers both the insurer and OSHA filings from the facts it gathers.

Pactum's AI chatbot runs supplier negotiations with Walmart's long-tail vendors on its own, within a value function that analysts define. Results go straight into ERP/CRM, and 3 out of 4 suppliers said they preferred it to a human. Its scope is still limited to commodity items, though.

In 2026, agentic procurement tools from Pactum, Keelvar, Arkestro and SAP Ariba contact and negotiate with hundreds of suppliers at once inside preset guardrails. Strategic contracts and escalations stay under human review.

Vendors and analysts describe tiered oversight: agents act alone on low-value spend, while a person picks among options for strategic sourcing and records why. That fits partial delegation rather than full delegation.

Agentic AI in hotels is being used to coordinate housekeeping scheduling, guest requests, distribution and revenue management. Agents can query the property management system and open maintenance tickets, but only about 1 in 10 chains uses agents at scale, and the specific savings figures come from vendor blogs.

Vendor material says agents check the property management system in real time and either answer a request or start a workflow such as a maintenance ticket. Inspecting and fixing the problem is still left to staff on site.
Lodging manager job postings include physically inspecting the facility, rooms and grounds, doing preventive maintenance, landscaping and overseeing check-in and check-out.

A 2025 WSP case study presented at IAIA describes an AI workflow for environmental baseline studies. It flags outdated datasets, fills gaps with remote sensing and uses text and data mining. This shows that agents can do the desk-based design and data-gathering steps.

A November 2025 ISEP advice note says AI adoption in environmental impact assessment is still uneven. A June 2026 UK scoping report includes a statement disclosing its AI use. Together they show AI assisting EIA scoping while practitioners keep responsibility for the work.

Under US agency NEPA rules, such as the Interior rule at 43 CFR 46.107, a Responsible Official must independently evaluate contractor-prepared environmental work, give written concurrence and remain responsible for the documents. A human therefore has to review and sign off.

UT Austin's open-source AI-assisted cataloging project builds metadata from images of items, searches OCLC WorldCat for matching records and has an LLM score each match. Catalogers still review the matches before batch upload, so a human stays in the loop.
OCLC already uses machine learning at scale on WorldCat bibliographic records. It ran AI de-duplication of records in 2025 and later extended it to all formats and languages.

A May 2026 industry post (secondary source) says OCLC added AI suggestions for classification and subject headings to Record Manager and Connexion, saving up to about 20 minutes per title in pilots. It also says OCLC's Bibliographic Formats and Standards now explains how to record AI-generated metadata, which implies human oversight.
Pharmacy software already produces the reorder lists from PAR or min/max levels. That covers the digital step before restocking but not putting stock on the shelves.
In this job description, aides restock shelves throughout the pharmacy and refill supplies to set inventory levels. Both are hands-on duties done under pharmacist supervision.
O*NET lists restocking storage areas and replenishing shelves as a separate task from receiving and inventorying medications.

Kitchen display system (KDS) expo screens only handle the information side of the hand-off. They flag front-of-house staff when all items in an order are done, but a person still carries the plates to the pass.
Expo screens list each dish as it finishes so servers don't have to check whether it is ready. That covers the coordination messages, not the physical passing of food.
Kitchen staff mark items done by 'bumping' them on the KDS, which tells servers the food is ready. The software tracks status but never moves the food.
Toast's help article describes the server printing an itemized receipt and leaving it with the guest. Guests can also view the itemized check on their phone, so the POS already builds the check.
Voice AI ordering agents connect to POS systems such as Toast, Square and Clover. They send captured orders and modifiers into the POS, where pricing and totals are handled.
With QR ordering, guests add items straight onto the same check in the POS, so no server has to enter them. Splitting checks and printing them happen on the floor.

Payment at restaurant tables is being automated by dedicated pay-at-table hardware such as NCR Voyix Aloha Pay-At-Table and the tabletop kiosks Chili's uses. These are fixed systems that replace the task, not a general AI agent doing the worker's job.

Self-checkout and self-order kiosks with AI features, such as Partner Tech's Paula, need physical card terminals or tabletop devices. Accepting payment at the counter means being there in person to handle cash, cards and receipts, which a software-only agent cannot do. It can only help with the digital steps in the POS system.

Vendor reports say 66% of US consumers prefer self-service kiosks to staffed checkouts (a figure from the vendor itself). This shows how payment is moving to kiosks rather than to agents running the register.

Digital tools automate developmental screening steps such as ASQ-3 delivery and scoring, and there are AI video-based screening apps for parents. But screening flags still need professional judgement and are meant to start a conversation, not stand alone.

Childcare programs use ASQ to identify developmental and social-emotional concerns, and it depends on adults directly observing the child. An agent can score the questionnaires or draft messages, but it cannot watch children in the room.

Childcare providers are mandated reporters for abuse. Developmental concerns are raised with parents through direct conversations, meetings, email or phone, which is a trust-based, in-person part of the job.

Caregiver apps such as Daily Nanny produce daily and weekly reports from logged naps, feeds, diapers and activities. These can support a parent check-in, but the nanny still has to log the data and hold the conversation.

Kidscare AI advertises AI journaling and milestone tagging to improve communication with parents about a child's development. This helps with preparation, but the content still comes from the caregiver's own firsthand observations.
Some systems, such as MyKidReports, generate the daily report automatically at checkout. That automates written updates, not the regular two-way meeting in which a nanny and parents build trust.
BLS says recreation workers do hands-on work such as setting up equipment, helping participants during activities, and cleaning and maintaining equipment or facilities.
O*NET lists 'Provide for entertainment and set up related decorations and equipment' as one of the occupation's tasks.

AI tools can suggest themes, decor concepts, checklists and shopping lists, which covers only the planning part. Hanging decorations, setting up equipment and running the entertainment still need a person on site.

Conversational AI agents can already sell event tickets end to end in chat. They recommend events, handle seat selection and run checkout for venues and ticketing platforms. This covers remote or digital sales channels only, not the counter.

AI agents are expected to automate ticket-buying steps such as queueing for ticket releases, comparing prices and making the purchase. The digital transaction side of selling tickets can be automated.

2026 AI customer-service agents can understand what the customer wants, pull account data and carry out actions such as payments and refunds within the conversation. At a cashier's counter, a person still has to take cash, hand over printed tickets or goods and scan items, which needs a physical presence.

Riff describes an agent that finds open purchase orders with no supplier confirmation, sends follow-ups to suppliers on its own, updates the ERP (SAP S/4HANA, Oracle, Dynamics 365) and escalates to a buyer when a supplier doesn't respond. This is the vendor's own claim and has not been tested independently.

Fellowmind describes a Supplier Communication Agent that sorts incoming supplier emails into confirmations, change requests and rejections, then shows the proposed ERP changes to a person for review before applying them. So changes still need a human step. This is the vendor's own claim and has not been tested independently.

SAP says Lemvigh-Müller's agents read supplier responses and compare quantities, dates and prices against purchase orders in SAP Cloud ERP. Mismatches are sent to follow-up workflows or flagged for a buyer to review. This is a customer story published by the vendor, with no independent measured results.
Stayntouch says its PMS sends a room's 'dirty' status to housekeepers' mobile devices when the folio closes at checkout, and then assigns cleaning tasks automatically. This is a vendor claim.
Oracle OPERA's documentation describes a setting that changes a room's housekeeping status automatically at checkout, so front desk staff don't have to set it by hand.

Mews MakeUpMyRoom reorders the housekeeping queue as soon as a checkout is logged in Mews. This is a vendor claim. Remaining cases, such as guests who leave without checking out, may still need a staff member to confirm the room is empty.

Libraries already run chatbots that point users to databases, help them search the catalog and answer questions about library services. Examples are Ask ALEX at the University of Oklahoma and ELIZA at Mahasarakham University. They are available around the clock, but no independent study has checked how accurate they are.

Job specifications say library assistants greet and help patrons at a front counter or public desk and show them where library services and materials are. Much of this instruction happens in person, on site.
No licence or certification is needed. Postings ask for a high school diploma plus experience, so no law requires a human to do or sign off on the task.

Vendors describe AI receptionists that answer calls, work out why the person is calling, apply routing rules and connect them to the right person, team or queue. They hand the call to a human when the caller asks or when the AI can't help. These sources are vendor marketing, and no independent accuracy benchmarks were found.

Virtual reception systems check visitors in and alert the host by SMS, email or chat. When a case is more complex, they connect the visitor to a live receptionist by video. This means walk-in visitors still partly need a human or physical kiosk hardware.
AI front-desk products say they welcome and verify visitors and notify hosts automatically at check-in, while sources note that AI still struggles to show empathy to stressed or confused visitors.

Prepress systems such as Enfocus PitStop Server already ingest files without a person: they watch hot folders, check incoming PDFs against preflight profiles and sort them into pass and fail folders with reports. Switch can also pull jobs from email, FTP and cloud services.
Kodak Prinergy ships Smart Hot Folder setups that are fully or semi-automatic for bringing jobs into the prepress workflow.

In 2026, computer-use agents can operate desktop apps with mouse and keyboard to enter and move data. This covers the keyboard and mouse part of the task, but someone still has to place physical originals on the scanner or in front of the camera.

A Morgan Lewis analysis from 2026 says AI agents are coming into labor relations work but will not replace labor negotiators or employee relations professionals. Unions are also pushing back on algorithmic management and bargaining over its use.
UK legal guidance in 2026 says AI can support HR and management decisions on grievances but should not replace human judgement. Acas is consulting on whether its grievance code should cover AI use.

Under the NLRA, meetings with employees and union representatives come with legal representation rights (Weingarten). These are person-to-person dealings between management and labor, not document processing.
O*NET lists this as a core hand-packer task: mark and label containers, container tags, or products using marking tools, alongside physical handling duties such as forklifts and pallet jacks.

Label printing software already designs labels, fills in their data from WMS, ERP or e-commerce systems, and prints them automatically from triggers or APIs. A software agent could therefore handle the digital part (label content and printing), but a person or a print-and-apply machine still has to put the label on the item.
SHRM's hand packer job description treats marking and labeling as manual physical work. Standard sources mention no licence or sign-off requirement for this task.

O*NET lists 'Load materials and products into package processing equipment' as a task for Packers and Packagers, Hand (53-7064.00). The occupation is defined as packing or packaging a wide variety of products and materials by hand, which is physical manipulation work.

The occupation's related tasks are also physical (examining, weighing, sealing and labeling containers). The reference agent has no robotics, so it can do at most minor digital support like looking up loading specs, not a substantial part of the task.

Batesville's Family Choices Digital Showroom is an online tool that guides families through choosing burial and cremation products. It suggests products based on information gathered in conversation, shows choices in real-time 3D and links to ordering. Software can therefore present product information without a person, but it does not maintain the physical casket display.

Funeral home software such as Passare and the tools listed on Capterra includes product catalogs that can be shared online and online arrangement features. One funeral director said these tools are not easy to use for showing caskets in the arrangement room, which suggests in-person showing is still the norm.

The FTC Funeral Rule requires funeral homes to give a General Price List to anyone who asks about goods, services or prices in person. They must also offer a casket price list before showing caskets, and give accurate prices to people who ask by phone. The rule sets how the information must be disclosed, but it does not require a licensed person to give it.

The funeral director normally gathers pallbearers 10–20 minutes before the service for an in-person rehearsal. During the service the director cues them aloud or by gesture and shows them where to place their hands when loading the casket. This on-site part needs a physical presence that an AI agent can't provide.

Funeral home case-management and family-portal software, such as Passare, Procession and Tukios, already handles scheduling and sends arrangement updates and notifications. An agent could use these tools to recruit and confirm pallbearers and send them written instructions. I found no feature built specifically for pallbearers.
Funeral-home guides describe the director as the person who instructs pallbearers. None of the sources say a licence or law requires a licensed person to arrange or brief them.

Affirmative action plan software already handles the data collection, analysis and reporting for equal-opportunity compliance, such as flagging underrepresentation and tracking progress toward goals. These analytic and drafting sub-steps can be done digitally. The source is a low-authority page.

Under 41 CFR 60-2, as of the 2022 legal alerts, covered US federal contractors had to certify through OFCCP's registration portal that they had developed and maintained their affirmative action programs. The results do not name the signatory, but the certification is an organizational legal representation, which points to a human accountability step. Whether the requirement still applies in 2026 was not confirmed; it was not verified here, but EO 11246 was reportedly revoked in January 2025, which would reduce this barrier.
The EEOC has warned that using AI does not excuse employers from liability for employment decisions. That makes human review of AI-generated appraisal and equity programs necessary before use.

O*NET lists 'Perform minor repairs and routine cleaning of audio and video equipment' as a core task for Audio and Video Technicians. Next to it is 'Notify supervisors when major equipment repairs are needed', so the work is hands-on upkeep of physical gear.
AI-assisted AV monitoring platforms analyze incidents and logs, suggest fixes and automate approved remote workflows. They help with diagnosis but cannot clean equipment or make physical repairs.

Remote AV monitoring gives per-device telemetry (lamp hours, power state, input errors) and remote commands. The vendor claims this cuts unnecessary on-site visits, but a technician still has to go on site to fix physical faults.

Broadcast automation systems commonly have a traffic or scheduling layer that builds program logs and feeds a playout layer that produces as-run logs. This means scheduling and reading logs is already digital, structured work done in software.
Aiir Scheduler can generate and export up to 30 days of music logs automatically, so log scheduling is already largely automated.

Playout vendors sell AI-driven scheduling that recommends the order of content. This is vendor marketing, but it shows the sub-steps are machine-executable. Final on-air and recording decisions and handling last-minute changes still usually need a technician in the control room to review them.

A global survey of practice found that contact lens application and removal training sessions took a median of 30 minutes. Lenses were usually dispensed only after the instructor watched the patient apply and remove them successfully three times. This is hands-on, in-person supervision.

Nevada requires dispensing optician applicants to log 15 hours of insertion and removal training on a record signed by a supervisor. The UK College of Optometrists requires a witness to confirm that a trainee can insert and remove a lens on a patient's eye safely. Both make this a licensed, physical competency.

Some AI tools already cover parts of the task. J&J Vision's 'Andy' chatbot answers questions about insertion, removal and lens care. The 'Lensie' app says it uses camera tracking to give real-time coaching on insertion. That claim comes from the developer and has not been validated.

O*NET lists 'Clean and organize work area and disinfect equipment after treatment' as a core task for Physical Therapist Aides (31-2022.00). Related tasks include changing linens and setting up equipment, which are also hands-on physical work.

APTA guidance says to clean all equipment, devices and surfaces between patients, following CDC disinfection recommendations. This means wiping physical surfaces at the point of care, which a software-only agent cannot do. An agent could at most look up the disinfection steps or keep the cleaning log.

Under infection-control manuals, shared equipment is disinfected at the point of care between each use, following the manufacturer's instructions. No law requires a licensed person to do this work, but it must be done in person.

O*NET lists the task as 'Assist patients to dress, undress, or put on and remove supportive devices, such as braces, splints, or slings.' Aides do it under close supervision of a physical therapist or physical therapy assistant, which means hands-on physical help with patients who may be injured.
A state job specification lists 'assist patients with dressing and undressing; apply and remove braces and splints' among the aide's in-person patient-care duties.

An employer job posting describes aides removing and replacing braces, splints and slings on patients' bodies before and after treatment. This is direct physical work that a software-only agent cannot do.

O*NET lists offering assistance to mourners as they enter or exit limousines as a Funeral Attendant task. The same profile includes other hands-on duties such as driving funeral vehicles and supervising processions.
SHRM's sample job description says attendants help mourners into and out of limousines, funeral vehicles and other transportation. This is done in person, physically and with compassion.
Alberta's occupational profile says the role has physical demands, including heavy lifting of over 50 kg.

Consumer AI climbing apps such as Climbah, Bouldering AI: Coach and MoveCl say they analyze uploaded videos for body position, foot placement and technique, and give feedback and training plans. That helps with coaching. Showing a skill in person, checking harnesses and knots, and spotting a climber still need a human on site. These capabilities come from app store listings and have not been independently verified.

MoveCl's listing says it detects 28 climbing techniques with pose estimation and scores them against ideal form. This shows AI can help with feedback on technique, but it cannot give hands-on instruction or demonstrate equipment.

Forum posts (not authoritative) say AMGA certification is not legally required in the US. They also say insurers and land permits in practice expect certified or vouched-for guides, so liability for the safety of people being taught sits with a human guide. I did not confirm any statute.
Crafco's Model 30 pavement router is a walk-behind machine. A worker on site steers it by an adjustable handle, and an electric clutch starts and stops the cutter-head.
A Cimline patent says the router operator has to keep raising and lowering the cutting bits when moving between random cracks. Doing this task means handling the machine by hand in real time.

Marathon's CR250KL crack router is a 20-25 hp engine-driven machine with carbide router blades. It is field equipment run by a person on the pavement and has no software interface that an agent could operate remotely.

O*NET lists this task for Highway Maintenance Workers (47-4051.00). Related duties include driving heavy equipment and vehicles with attachments to sweep debris from paved surfaces, and setting out signs and cones to divert traffic. The work is physical, done on site and with equipment.

The occupation's core duties are hands-on field work: clearing debris from culverts, ditches and drains, hauling material to fill washouts, and driving trucks to work sites. A software-only agent with no body cannot do any of these.

The typical entry route is a high school diploma plus moderate-term on-the-job training. No professional licence requires a human to sign off on debris removal itself, though heavy vehicles may need a CDL.

The only automation found for changing drill bits and loading bolts on roof bolters is mechanical: carousels and manipulators described in patents and controlled by machine controllers. That is robotics hardware, not a software agent, and on conventional machines operators still reload by hand.

Patents for autonomous roof bolters describe drilling and bolting sequences run by controllers and physical loading arms on the machine. A software-only AI with no body cannot do the physical work of pulling a bit from a chuck and seating a bolt underground.

A newer patent describes a controller that rotates the carousel to swap consumables such as drill bits, resin cartridges and bolts. This confirms the task is manual handling at the drill head in an underground mine.

AI drowning-detection systems such as Lynxight and AngelEye watch pool camera feeds and send alerts to lifeguards' smartwatches. They are presented as an extra layer of safety, not a replacement for lifeguards, and they only work at pools that already have the cameras installed.
Industry bodies treat AI drowning detection as a supplement to lifeguard supervision and are still working out how to fit it into existing supervision frameworks.
Florida law requires anyone working as a lifeguard at a public pool to hold a certificate from the American Red Cross, the YMCA, or another nationally recognized aquatic training program.

Zoos move animals between enclosures and into transport crates through hands-on shift and crate training led by keepers in person: targeting, positive reinforcement and handling the doors. That is physical work an agent without a body cannot do.
Moving an animal depends on keepers reading its behaviour on the spot and dealing with social or environmental problems, for example separating individuals or adding visual barriers.
Software such as Species360 ZIMS covers only the paperwork side: recording transfers and visits. An agent could help there, but that is a small part of the time the task takes.

Ticketing software can track exits and re-entries: scanning a ticket on the way out makes it valid again for coming back in, so the system does the record-keeping part of a door check. Staff still operate the scanner at the door.
For multi-day or high-volume events, vendors recommend physical credentials such as wristbands or hand stamps that staff check by eye at the door. That means a person has to be physically present.
At large venues, guests ask staff for a re-entry wristband when they leave and must show it with their ticket when they return.

Building a new bike from the box means handling the parts by hand: mounting wheels, seatpost, bar and stem, aligning the derailleur and brake calipers, and tightening bolts to spec with a torque wrench. An AI agent with no robot body can't do this. At most it can look up the manufacturer's instructions and torque specs.
Brake setup means holding the lever in while tightening the caliper bolts to 8 Nm, then spinning the wheel to check for rotor drag. These are hands-on adjust-and-check steps.

Under 16 CFR 1512.3, a bike sold partly assembled must meet federal safety requirements once it is put together according to the manufacturer's instructions. The rule sets a product standard and does not require a licensed or certified person to assemble it.

HR AI agents in 2026 handle recruiting (screening, scheduling), onboarding (provisioning, document tracking, FAQs) and performance (data aggregation, coaching nudges), with claimed cuts in HR admin time of up to 40% (vendor-reported).
About one in three organizations uses AI for first-round video or voice screening interviews, and AI scheduling tools reportedly cut coordinator time by 36%.

Postmasters recruit, interview, select, hire, train, supervise and evaluate post office staff, and select and train postmasters of associate units. This includes on-site on-the-job training and a final hiring decision made by an accountable manager.

The BLUPF90 suite is standard software for mixed-model analysis in animal breeding. It estimates variance components and heritability by REML, including standard errors, and it can be run from scripts, so an agent with code execution can do the core estimation.
UNE lab handouts show that AI-REML in blupf90+ reports standard errors for heritability and genetic correlations. This is a routine computational workflow.

bpf90tools is a Python wrapper built to automate breeding-value pipelines (renumf90, remlf90, airemlf90). The search found no turnkey end-to-end system, so a human still needs to choose the model and check the results.

NWCG Crew Boss (CRWB) qualification requires prior Firefighter Type 1 experience, a certified Position Task Book, specific courses (RT-130, S-230, S-290, ICS-200) and an arduous fitness level, so a qualified human must lead fire crews.
The CRWB role involves running, climbing and lifting over 50 lb, plus real-time decisions in the field, such as judging changing fire conditions and deciding when to withdraw a crew.

Digital tools such as VR forest-worker training and AI wildfire-planning platforms support training and planning, but they do not lead crews in the field. AI can only help with training materials, scheduling and briefings.

Commercial AI course-design tools available in 2026 (ibl.ai Course AI, Coursebox, Taskade) produce syllabi, weekly plans, learning objectives, rubrics and assignments from a course description, map content to accreditation outcomes and export to LMSs. These sources are vendor marketing with no independent quality data, and all of them assume a human reviews the output.

A 2025 case study describes a graduate course built quickly with generative AI to meet an accreditation deadline, including AI-generated syllabus, lecture and homework files. Faculty still had to direct and refine the work.

University governance gives faculty responsibility for curriculum. Course proposals start with a faculty member and pass through department, college and university committee approval. This is institutional governance, not a legal licence or signature requirement.

AI agent add-ons for Canvas can send scores straight to the Canvas gradebook through LTI grade passback. Canvas stays the official record for enrollment and grades, and other platforms already send session attendance to the gradebook automatically.
A news report says Instructure is rolling out an agentic AI assistant in Canvas that automates routine teaching work such as basic grading and rubric creation.

Nursing programs treat clinical evaluations and competency records as FERPA-protected education records. Access is limited to the course instructor and coordinators, so a human instructor stays responsible for certifying and controlling these records.

Some education platforms such as KUNSTMATRIX.EDU, Artsteps and Artsonia let users build and publish 3D or online exhibitions of student work in a browser, with role-based access. An agent could upload the work, lay out the gallery and write the labels without a human doing each step.
Schools commonly use online galleries such as Artsonia, ART.SPACES and website exhibition pages to show student art. This supports digital delegation of the display and promotion sub-steps.

Physical shows in schools and galleries require handling, hanging, lighting and installing artworks on site. No law or licence requires a human to sign off, but the physical installation and the curatorial choices are still human steps.

AI teacher tools such as MagicSchool's lesson planner produce full standards-aligned lesson plans, with objectives, activities, assessments and differentiation, from a short goal description. This covers the planning sub-step end to end, though a teacher still reviews and adapts the plan.
Oklahoma's law effective July 1, 2026 keeps classroom AI use educator-directed. This shows K-12 policy keeps a human teacher in charge of instruction.

A Pennsylvania bill would require certified human teachers, not AI, as the primary instructor in charter schools. California AB 2370 already bars AI from replacing community-college instructors of record. Both point to a human-in-charge rule for instruction.
AI dispatch and routing software plans the order of stops, re-plans routes during the day and assigns jobs to drivers. That only supports the human courier, who still carries every item to the door.
Courier platforms offer smart dispatch that assigns the nearest available driver based on location, load capacity and availability. The physical delivery is still done by a person.
Autonomous delivery robots are a separate robotics technology studied in research. They fall outside a software-only AI agent with no physical body.

Most movable bridges are worked from a local control console with physical switches, signals and gates. Remote operation exists at a few sites (WisDOT Sturgeon Bay since 2011, Canal & River Trust). Even there, a human operator watches CCTV, checks the deck is clear and starts the sequence. Lasers block the barriers from lowering if people or vehicles are on the deck, which shows how much depends on safety checks.

The federal traffic manual (MUTCD) Standard says signals, gates and movable spans shall be controlled by the bridge tender through an interlocked control. Responsibility therefore sits with a human tender.

Remote setups depend on site cameras, PLCs, safety-rated (SIL2) control systems and dedicated fiber links. These are closed industrial control networks that a general AI agent would not normally be able to reach. Early remote trials also had trouble judging distance and dealing with headlight glare on camera at night.
OptimoRoute sells automated route planning for garbage and waste collection that takes driver skills, breaks and vehicle limits into account.
Wastehero's Route AI turns collection schedules into routes automatically, using vehicle capacity, time windows and road limits, and syncs them with the office in real time.

Dayjob AI pulls data from waste ERP systems to build next-day schedules and has an in-day planner for changes. A human still has to set the rules and approve the plan, and the work depends on access to company dispatch systems.

Vendor tools describe AI agents that read a client brief, pull comparable past proposals and draft scope, timelines and pricing. They claim this cuts scoping time by 40-60%, but these figures are unverified vendor claims.

Planning agents (Taskade's three-agent team, Microsoft Planner Agent) generate scope, timeline and resource plans from briefs or meeting notes. Guidance still stresses that a human applies judgment to the plan.
The CMC is a voluntary professional designation, not a government licence. Only use of the title is regulated, for example in Alberta, so no law requires a human to plan or sign a study.

Parks already use AI assistants to answer visitor questions about routes, permits, hours and safety, usually in several languages. Examples include Gran Paradiso's Sibilla, the Mysuru Zoo assistant and Frisco's park avatar. Most of these accounts are written by the vendors, and I found no confirmed chatbot run by a US state wildlife agency.

State job descriptions say wardens give information and education to the public on statutes and regulations while doing field enforcement on patrol. That means they mostly advise visitors face to face, on site, during patrols.

Warden duties include patrolling by car, boat, plane, horse or on foot and making daily contact with many outside groups. In that setting, advice is given in person, in the moment, and with the authority of the badge.

Motorola Solutions' Assist tools transcribe field radio traffic and suggest incidents to dispatchers. This speeds up the communication and logging part of the task, but a human dispatcher still confirms the incident.

In 2026, police agencies such as San Diego County Sheriff, La Mesa and El Cajon use AI voice agents (Hyper, Aurelian Ava) to take and route non-emergency complaints. These calls include parking issues, and humans review the intake or receive the hand-off.

Motorola bought Hyper in April 2026 and sells agentic AI for public-safety call handling. This automates the dispatcher side of the exchange, not the field officer who answers the radio call and goes to the scene.

Camera traps with AI (Microshare EverSmart, BrightAI/Pelsis) can identify species and counts and send alerts. This only supports monitoring at fixed devices; the worker still has to walk the premises, find the source and judge structural damage and entry points.
In Washington State, inspecting for pests, their signs or conducive conditions requires a WSDA licence. WDO reports for property transfers must carry state-issued inspection control numbers.
Florida Stat. 482.226 requires the licensee or a qualified representative to produce wood-destroying organism inspection reports on a state-prescribed form.

Starting a horse means training it to accept a saddle, bridle and rider and to respond to rein and voice cues. A trainer has to be physically with the horse, handling it on the ground and riding it, to do this; software cannot.

Starting a horse to harness also means hands-on work with the horse and the equipment, step by step. An AI agent without a body could at most suggest a training plan, which is a tiny share of the working time.

Barco Insights is a cloud platform for projectors. It shows live usage and environmental data, health history and log-file review, and sends health-issue alerts through email and an API. An agent could run this digital part of the pre-show check from start to finish.

Barco's NOC already monitors networked cinema projectors, servers, theatre management systems and UPS units remotely, and can analyse and upgrade them remotely. One exhibitor has more than 160 projectors monitored this way across 12 sites.

Christie's NOCs monitor projectors, players and theatre management systems around the clock, and use predictive maintenance tools to spot problems early. Physical checks such as lens and port-glass cleanliness, focus, film path and mechanical condition still need a person on site.

O*NET lists 'Install and connect auxiliary equipment, such as microphones, amplifiers, disc playback machines, and lights' as a supplemental task for Motion Picture Projectionists (39-3021.00). The work means physically mounting, cabling and connecting hardware. An agent without a body cannot do that. It can only help with wiring diagrams, manuals, signal-flow planning and troubleshooting advice.
O*NET describes the occupation as setting up and operating projection and related sound reproduction equipment, which is hands-on work in the booth and auditorium.

AI shade-matching, virtual try-on and personalized product recommendation tools (Perfect Corp/MAKE UP FOR EVER, ModiFace) already handle advisory sub-steps of makeup selling, but they support the in-person sale rather than complete it.
Retailers have deployed virtual makeup try-on at scale (L'Oréal ModiFace on Amazon; Watsons offering try-on for 300 products), so the digital part of recommending and selling makeup can be automated.

Selling makeup at a counter generally needs no esthetician license, but applying makeup on clients for pay can count as licensed esthetics practice. Salon selling usually involves hands-on demonstration and in-person persuasion.

Commercial camera-and-AI systems already score lameness and body condition automatically. CattleEye says its system monitors more than 150,000 cattle using a camera at the milking parlour exit. These systems need fixed farm hardware and cover only some signs of illness, not a full hands-on exam.

Research systems detect cattle lameness from a single side-view camera in real time using Mask-RCNN and YOLOv8. A software agent could analyse such video feeds, but palpation, taking temperatures and handling the animal still need a person on site.
Nedap's SmartSight computer-vision product monitors livestock health with farm cameras. This supports AI help with spotting symptoms, but the breeder still does the physical examination.
Shows take entries online during set windows and accept no late entries (Milam County, TX; Kent County, DE uses the Showman system). An agent could handle this paperwork and deadline work.
Entry forms need each animal's name, birth date, breed and registration number, which is document work an AI can prepare. Showing the animal itself still happens in person in the ring.
Showmanship must be done with the same animal entered in that species' market class, so a person has to handle that animal physically in the ring.

CattleMax and other herd-management software already track semen inventory (owned and non-owned bulls, tank location, collection codes) and connect breeding and pregnancy records. The logging and record-keeping steps are already digital, so an agent could run them.

Digital Beef has a semen module that records AI breeding data, semen usage and tank or canister location. An agent could fill in and reconcile these records once it has the breeding-event data, which is created in the barn when someone inseminates an animal and reads its ID.

Form-based apps let breeders and vets record semen use on mobile devices on site. Someone physically present still has to capture the event (which straw went into which animal), so a human supplies or checks the source data.

Animals are identified with physical ear tags (840 RFID, NUES metal or plastic button tags), brands and tattoos. Someone has to restrain each animal and apply the tag or mark by hand. The software-friendly part of the job is getting a premises ID and keeping records.

USDA's proposal to require RFID tags for interstate cattle movement by 2023 was withdrawn. Brands and tattoos can still count as official ID if the shipping and receiving states agree. The rules set which ID methods are accepted, not who may apply them, so no licence is needed to do the tagging.

To get official tags, a producer needs a premises identification number (PIN) from the state. This registration and tag-record step is the only part an AI agent could do; branding, tattooing and tagging the animal itself needs a body and hands.
O*NET lists 'Cut and install insulating or sound-absorbing material' as a task for Helpers--Carpenters (47-3012.00), an occupation that helps carpenters with lower-skill hands-on duties
DOL job postings for carpenter helpers list this task next to other on-site physical work such as cutting lumber and holding materials for fastening
Occupation profile confirms the work is manual and done on construction sites, so a software-only agent with no body cannot cut or install material

Hot vulcanizing is hands-on work: the worker places the patch over the puncture, protects the tube, clamps the press arm, switches on the heater, then waits about ten minutes for the tube to cool before taking it out. An agent with no robotic body cannot do any of this.

Hot patches are cured by heat and pressure from a heated plate that presses the tube onto the patch, with a controlled rise and fall in temperature. The work is done with a physical tool and the rubber itself, not through software.

Before patching, the tube is scuffed and the patch clamped onto it by hand, so every main step needs physical handling. AI could only help a little, such as looking up cure times in the manufacturer's instructions. I found no licence requirement for this work.

O*NET lists hands-on work as the core of this job: adjusting shutters, light meters and lens systems with hand tools, taking equipment apart to find defects, testing with precision gauges, and reading engineering drawings. Advising on equipment design draws on what the repairer sees during this physical work, which an agent cannot do itself.

Industry AI reasoning agents already go through past work orders and failure events and produce recommendations with cost and risk tradeoffs, which engineers then test before acting. That covers the analysis and write-up steps of a design-change recommendation, but humans still review the result.

Generative AI reliability assistants are described as adding to maintenance practice while keeping human expertise and oversight, so human review of engineering recommendations is still expected. I found no licensing or sign-off rule that applies to camera repairers.

Dedicated PLC-controlled autowinders already switch reels and cut at a preset length. Setting them up, threading the product, and handling and weighing the reels are still done by hand on the shop floor. A software-only AI agent cannot do any of that physical work.

Conair's ATC coilers change spindles automatically once the programmed footage is reached and save recipes. The only digital part an AI agent could help with is choosing or entering recipe parameters, and that depends on access to the machine's HMI.

Dedicated computer-vision systems at the dock (e.g., Accella Dock Check) can count cases, read barcodes and flag pallet discrepancies before shipment. These are fixed-camera installations that sit on site, not something a general software agent can reach.
Vision AI can detect broken boards, leaning stacks and loaded vs. empty pallets, but only if cameras and models have been set up for that site. This covers a small part of what a supervisor checks.

Reviewing hand-labor work as it happens and once it is finished mostly means walking the site and checking stacking, cleanup, loading and safety in person. An agent with no body can only help by reviewing photos, scanner logs or WMS records the supervisor is able to share.

EMS inventory software can track par levels and usage for each vehicle, raise restock alerts and send digital orders to suppliers. That covers the planning and ordering side, but not putting supplies on the ambulance.
ESO's inventory tools use min/max par levels and usage data to decide what to reorder. Restocking the truck itself is still done by crew members by hand.
AngelTrack's supply-room software tracks stock moving between stations and checks that each ambulance is stocked before it leaves. People still have to load the vehicle.

Lattice's agent (2026) drafts performance reviews from months of performance data that is already in the system. By design, it never picks a rating and never submits a review on its own, so the manager stays accountable.

Lattice MCP, released July 2026, lets managers draft, edit and submit reviews from inside Claude, ChatGPT or Slack. An agent can reach the performance data and handle the drafting sub-steps from start to finish.
The EU AI Act treats AI used for promotion or termination decisions as high-risk and requires qualified human oversight. Compliance may be delayed to December 2027, but the classification stays.

AI scribes for therapy record the session, draft progress notes in formats such as SOAP, and place them in the EHR. Vendors also say clinicians must review, edit and approve each note before it is submitted.

Under California law, failing to keep records consistent with sound clinical judgment and professional standards is unprofessional conduct. This makes the licensed therapist responsible for the record.
Ontario's regulator requires every clinical record entry to show who made it and when, so the professional stays accountable for its contents.

Under prison use-of-force policies, the on-site supervisor approves planned force and decides what type and how much. Staff physically apply restraints and chemical agents, and the use is recorded on video.

In North Carolina, chemical agents may only be used with authorization from the facility head or a designee. They are handled by trained chemical officers who are sergeants or above, so a human with that rank has to authorize and carry out the use.
Prison AI tools such as Leo Technologies' Verus Vision AI only analyze video feeds and alert staff to incidents. They do not restrain or control anyone.

OSHA training material for housekeeping staff covers handling, diluting, storing and spilling cleaning chemicals, and wearing protective gear. These are hands-on steps a worker does on site. An AI agent can only help by looking up labels and safety data sheets or explaining the steps.

Some robot scrubbers and dispensing systems already measure and mix cleaning chemicals automatically. That is robot hardware, though, not a software-only AI agent, which is the technology being rated here.

OSHA's 1991 guidance letter applies its hazard communication rule to janitorial work. The rule puts the duty to train on the employer and does not require a licensed person to sign off on routine use of cleaning chemicals.

Chimney sweeping is hands-on work. CSIA certification covers chimney construction, NFPA 211 and cleaning technique, all done on site with brushes and tools. A software agent with no robotics cannot do any of it.
Sweeps generally do not need certification. It is recommended but optional, so the law does not require a human to perform or sign off on routine cleaning.
O*NET lists a Certified Chimney Sweep credential (exam plus renewal every 3 years). It is a voluntary professional credential, not a legal licence for cleaning.

Current AI landscape tools mostly produce designs and visualizations: planting schemes, layouts and plant suggestions based on site data. They help a worker read and understand a plan but do nothing on the ground.

Consumer AI landscaping apps are mainly photo-based idea generators or planners that set placement on screen. None of the material found describes an agent that marks or stakes out real planting locations on site.

AI tools aimed at landscape architects generate planting and grading proposals, which covers the design step the task starts from. Carrying out that design on the ground still takes a person working on site.

Agent templates for sales engineers already analyze client usage patterns and technical requirements, find upsell opportunities and produce tailored presentations on the ROI of recommended solutions. These are the main drafting and analysis sub-steps of this task.

Sales engineer roles involve regular customer site visits to learn about installed equipment and operating conditions, and to recommend equipment that improves productivity and profitability. That on-site understanding and persuasion is the input an agent cannot gather by itself.
A case study of a sales proposal agent reports that the time humans spent editing technical proposal drafts outweighed the time saved, so humans still had to review the work before use.

Agentic procurement platforms advertised for 2025–2026 claim to create requisitions, turn them into purchase orders, source vendors and buy low-risk, high-volume items on their own. These are vendor claims and have not been independently checked.
ServiceNow has announced autonomous procurement workflows that can run equipment and supply buying from start to finish inside enterprise systems.

Disposing of IT assets requires physical work: removing drives, keeping a chain of custody, and getting destruction certificates from certified vendors. An agent can arrange and document this, but people have to do the physical handling and check it on site. No law requires a supervisor to sign it personally.

USDA FNS lists New Mexico using robotic process automation to move client-portal data into the eligibility system, add case notes and create caseworker tasks. Code for America and Anthropic are building Claude-based tools for SNAP caseworkers that review documents and draft communications.

Code for America and Anthropic's SNAP Policy Navigator helps caseworkers look up policy, review eligibility documents and draft plain-language messages to recipients, with the caseworker still in the loop.

Under 7 CFR 272.4(a), SNAP certification work, including interviews and eligibility and benefit determinations, must be done by state merit-system staff. Nonmerit personnel cannot enter data into eligibility-affecting fields, so a human must review and own those records. The task needs no physical presence.

Log scanners already detect defects and assign quality grades automatically, for example MiCROTEC Logeye (laser, color imaging and X-ray with deep-learning AI) and SMARTI iLog. These are fixed sawmill machines with their own sensors, not software agents that only reach digital systems. A human grader in a log yard or landing still has to look at the logs in person: knots, sweep, rot and end defects.

SMARTI's iLog X-ray scanner builds 3D models of logs, detects surface and internal defects, and sorts logs into quality grades. It shows that grading done by sensors depends on dedicated physical hardware.

Idaho law makes it unlawful to scale logs for commercial purposes without a license from the Board of Scaling Practices, or to work as an apprentice except under a licensed scaler. Getting a license requires passing written and practical exams.

Camera-based and 3D log scanning systems for measuring logs and detecting defects exist, but they are still at the research or preliminary stage and need dedicated scanning hardware at the mill. Certified scalers are still used to check the results.
A USDA laser-scan system found 53 of 64 severe surface defects on hardwood logs and flagged 9 sound areas as defects. That is specialized hardware, not something a general software agent can operate.
In Idaho, anyone doing commercial log scaling must hold a license, which requires passing written and practical exams. Licensed scalers also face unannounced check scales.

Confined-space testing means a trained person takes a calibrated direct-reading meter to the space and samples it in a set order: oxygen first, then flammable gases, then toxic gases. An entry supervisor has to confirm the tests were done before signing the entry permit.

Cloud-connected detectors with pump cartridges, such as the Blackline G7, still need a worker on site to lower the probe and sample the space. The software only streams the readings and stores the record, which an agent could watch and use to fill in the paperwork.
Sample programs require monitoring for O2, LEL, H2S and CO, and require protecting the tester from the space's atmosphere while sampling. This is physical work done at the space.

Under FRA rules, railroads must designate qualified persons to inspect freight cars and decide whether they can safely move. Those people must show the railroad they have the knowledge and ability to do so, and the railroad must keep records of each designation.

AI and CMMS tools for rail fleets predict when components such as wheelsets will wear out and turn those predictions into prioritized work orders and maintenance schedules. They support planning, but they do not do the hands-on maintenance or cleaning.
Railcar wheelset analytics, such as Railinc/TransmetriQ, help owners set the mileage between repairs. The repair work itself is still physical work done by people in the shop.

Vendor AI support agents run step-by-step troubleshooting for electronics products (printers, laptops, peripherals). They ask diagnostic questions, give targeted fixes and automate warranty and RMA intake. These are vendor claims.

When electrical equipment needs hands-on guidance, a remote human expert directs the on-site operator over live video with AR annotations. The instruction can be given remotely, but complex or safety-critical cases still rely on expert human judgment.
AR 'see-what-I-see' tools let a remote party guide customers through repairs, so instructing does not require being there in person. It is mostly human-led today.

O*NET lists this as a core task for Structural Metal Fabricators and Fitters: aligning and fitting parts with jacks, turnbuckles, wedges, drift pins, pry bars and hammers. That is hands-on work with tools on heavy steel.

Automated fit-up systems such as the PeddiAssembler (robotic tacking, parts scanning, laser measurement) do exist. They are dedicated robotic hardware, though, not software AI agents, so they fall outside the reference technology, which has no physical body.
Robotics has been less common in structural steel shops because steel framing projects are highly customized, so most fit-up is still done by hand.
OSHA 1910.218 requires that before dies are changed on forging presses, the pumps and power equipment are locked out and the ram is blocked. A person has to do this hands-on at the machine.
California Title 8 §4242 requires lockout, a flywheel at rest and ram blocking with rated material when dies are changed on forging and hot trimming presses.
Removing dies means unclamping them and moving heavy dies with hoists and slings. This is physical rigging work that a software-only agent cannot do.

Automating die and tool setup takes dedicated machine hardware: automatic tool changers built into the press brake with robotic manipulators. Software alone does not do it. Without that hardware, setup means placing, aligning, shimming and clamping tooling by hand, which can take more than 30 minutes for complex layouts.

OSHA 1910.217(d) sets physical safety procedures for diesetters on mechanical power presses: lockout of power, inch mode, and moving the slide by hand. Die setting is in-person work at the machine. The rule sets safety requirements but does not require a license or signature.

Offline software such as DiamondBend can write tool setup programs. That is the only digital part a software agent could help with: looking up setup sheets or tooling layouts. A machine or a person still has to install and lock the tools physically.

MTConnect is an open, read-only standard. Its agents expose machine data items such as spindle speed and feed rate over HTTP, so software can log these values from networked machine tools without manual entry.
Commercial collectors poll the MTConnect /current stream at set intervals and save the values to a database automatically. This is the core 'record operational data' step for connected CNC equipment.

Data coverage depends on the controller: no single adapter exposes every NC data item, and FOCAS is used for Fanuc. On older or non-networked presses and gauges, someone still has to read the values physically at the machine.

Vendors sell dedicated vision systems: cameras with lighting fixtures and deep-learning models mounted on finishing lines that pass, reject or send plated parts for rework. They detect blistering, peeling and skip plating. This is fixed hardware, not a general software agent, and each line must be set up and calibrated in person.

A vendor says AI vision can flag air bubbles, dewetting and thin or missing coverage on coatings, but only with specialised lighting such as low-angle darkfield. Someone has to arrange the lighting and handle the part, which a bodiless agent can't do.
How well the model works depends on inspectors agreeing on defect labels before training. Humans still set the acceptance standard and judge borderline parts.

O*NET 51-9082.00: medical appliance technicians build and repair orthotic and prosthetic devices with hand and power tools, and one of their listed tasks is repairing production equipment or tools. The work is hands-on shop-floor repair.

Current agentic maintenance AI predicts faults, checks parts availability, drafts work orders and searches manuals to help technicians troubleshoot. People still approve the work and do the physical repair.
Generative AI's main near-term value in maintenance is helping technicians troubleshoot complex machines by searching large PDF manuals. Robotic repair is a separate, longer-term trend.

Truck-specific routing tools, such as NextBillion.ai's routing API, are marketed as building routes from vehicle height, weight and cargo type. They also claim to apply hazmat tunnel codes and bridge weight limits. This is vendor marketing and has not been independently verified.

Commercial truck navigation products also say they check every route against bridge heights, weight limits and hazmat restrictions. The pre-trip map reading and route choice can therefore be largely automated in software, though accuracy is unverified.

Under 49 CFR 397.67, hazmat routing duties fall on the motor carrier, and for some explosives a written route plan must be given to the driver. The rule does not require a human to personally read the map, but the driver remains responsible for checking the route against real conditions and adjusting it.

Vendor tools such as Veryon Guided Troubleshooting and Pratt & Whitney's AI borescope software already produce fix and replacement recommendations from fault and inspection data, but qualified engineers or inspectors review, correct and give final approval of the result.
AI predictive maintenance in airline MRO flags component wear such as cooling units early so a replacement can be scheduled, but people make the maintenance decisions.

Under 14 CFR 43.9, a maintenance or alteration record must carry the signature, certificate number and certificate type of the person approving the work, so a certificated human stays legally accountable.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.176 says storage areas must be kept clear of materials that create tripping, fire, explosion or pest hazards, and that stacked goods must be stabilized. Meeting this means physically cleaning, stacking and securing things on site. No human sign-off is required.

Commercial IoT sensor systems already watch warehouse temperature, humidity, flooding, smoke and entry, and send alerts. The task's digital part (watching conditions, flagging problems, writing checklists) can be supported or automated by software, but a person still has to act on each alert.
Industry guides describe warehouse monitoring as sensors, IoT and RFID tracking conditions and materials. They support inventory protection but do not replace the hands-on upkeep of storage areas.

Off-the-shelf tools (Scenario, 3D AI Studio using GPT Image 2, Nano Banana Pro, Flux Kontext turnaround LoRA) generate multi-view character turnaround and model sheets from one prompt or reference image, keeping the character consistent across views.

Character sheet generators turn a single image into a four-view grid. Vendors still advise checking consistency on your own characters, so a human still has to review and correct the sheet before production use.

The US Copyright Office won't register purely AI-generated images, and prompts alone don't count as human authorship. This affects who owns the character, not whether an agent can draw it, so no licence or signature is needed to do the task.
Agentic AI inventory tools forecast demand from POS sales and stock data and generate purchase orders. The setup vendors recommend has a manager review orders before they are sent.
BlueCart's predictive ordering uses depletion rates, real-time inventory and seasonal trends to suggest reorder quantities, which staff then approve.
Restaurants spend about 8 to 12 hours a week on manual stock counting and ordering. The physical count is still done by people unless sensors are installed.

Commercial tray-tracking software (Computrition Tray InMotion Elite) checks patient identity and diet orders automatically, tracks trays from ticket creation to delivery and alerts staff when diet orders change. The vendor says this helps prevent delivery mistakes, but this claim comes from marketing and has not been independently checked.

In a real hospital deployment, a staff member still scans the tray barcode and the patient's wristband with an iPad at the bedside before handing over the meal. The final match is still done in person.
Under a manual hospital policy, staff compare the diet order with the tray slip on the spot and ask the nurse to confirm when unsure. This is physical, on-site checking with no licence requirement.

evidence.fact: O*NET lists stocking service stations with ice, napkins and straws as a task for Food Servers, Nonrestaurant (35-3041.00). The work is physically carrying supplies and refilling them on site.
Server sidework checklists treat restocking stations with napkins, straws, silverware, ice and glasses as hands-on side work. Software can only help by tracking checklists or inventory.
Toast's server job description includes restocking server stations and refilling ice at the soda station, which takes a physical presence.

Food-carrying in restaurants is being automated, but by physical delivery robots such as PuduBot, not by software-only AI agents. Even with these robots, staff place the dishes on the robot by hand and enter the table numbers.

Moving dishes from the kitchen to a table or counter takes a body or a robot with a gripping arm, as with the Pudu A1. That is robotics, which falls outside the reference technology of software-only agents.

Bars use commercial underbar glasswashers that a person has to load, unload and run by hand, using either high-temperature (185°F rinse) or chemical sanitizing. These machines are physical equipment, not software an AI agent can operate.
Health rules for bars describe hands-on steps, such as fully immersing glassware in sanitizer of at least 25 ppm for at least two minutes. This document is an older local code from Albany, Oregon.
One spec sheet shows a unit that runs a 185°F sanitizing rinse every cycle. A person still has to collect, load and put away the glasses, which an agent without a body cannot do.

Smart irrigation controllers (Rachio, Rain Bird ARC, Hunter Hydrawise) already set watering schedules automatically from weather data. Only this small digital part of watering could go to software that an agent might configure; mulching, mowing, pruning, planting and fertilizing all need hands-on work on site.

In Florida, a landscape maintenance operator cannot apply pesticides without proper certification, and for-hire lawn fertilizer application needs a state license (GI-BMP training plus an exam). The person applying it must be licensed or work under a licensed operator's supervision.
Some cities add their own license for businesses that apply lawn fertilizer or pesticide, and the application lists each employee's state commercial applicator license number.
